prose.summary: Sound designers create and shape audio that supports an experience, story or interaction. They select, record, edit and organize sound so it works with timing and context. The current live sample is unusually narrow and reflects remote audio-expert contracts more than the full occupation.
prose.day_to_day: Typical work can involve editing source audio, building effects, reviewing timing and delivering files that fit a production pipeline. The live evidence, however, is limited to a handful of remote music or audio-expert contracts connected to AI research. It does not support a broad claim about current game, film or product-audio hiring.
prose.work_environment: Every opening in the tiny current sample is remote contract work, but that sample is not representative enough to define the occupation. Studio recording, field capture and production review may still require specialized spaces or shared sessions. Treat location claims cautiously.
prose.getting_in: Build a focused reel that shows the original material, your edit and the reason each sound supports the scene or interaction. Document file organization, revision and delivery, not only the final mix. Because the live evidence is thin, target employers should be checked directly for their software and format expectations.
prose.ladder: Early work handles defined assets, edits and implementation support. Responsibility can grow toward ownership of a scene, system or production audio language. The exact ladder varies sharply between games, film, interactive products and contract audio work.
prose.suits: This work fits people who notice timing, texture and unwanted noise and can revise repeatedly against a brief. It requires patience with detailed listening and technical delivery. It is a poor fit if the attraction is only music creation without production constraints.
prose.misconceptions: Sound design is not the same as composing music and not simply cleaning a recording. The work is about building purposeful audio behavior or atmosphere within a larger production.
prose.who_qualifies: Audio engineers, editors, musicians with production discipline and interactive-media creators may bring adjacent foundations. The current route data is too thin to rank those paths reliably. A reel and deliverable workflow remain the clearest proof.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: The live sample is tiny, contract-heavy and centered on AI audio expertise. It cannot show the broader demand, studio conditions or specialization mix of sound-design work.

steps.how: Focus on games, film, products or another target so the reel reflects a real delivery pipeline.
Preserve source material and explain the editing, layering and timing decisions behind the final sound.
Use clear naming, versions and export settings so another person can review and implement the work.
Ask whether the sound supports the intended scene or interaction rather than whether it sounds impressive alone.

prose.tools: The live files do not provide a reliable sound-tool profile. They show translation and language-related audio expertise in a small contract sample. Editing, recording and delivery tools should therefore be verified against the target production.

faq.q: what is the difference between sound design and audio engineering?
faq.a: Sound design creates and shapes audio for a specific experience, while audio engineering focuses more on recording, routing, mixing and technical sound quality. Many projects need both.
